title: In situ Scanning Transmission Electron Microscopy (STEM) Imaging of Atomic Behavior at Solid Liquid Interfaces Enabled by Deep Learning Data Analysis
content: In situ (scanning) transmission electron microscopy ((S)TEM) in liquids and gasses is a powerful method for studying materials in dynamic environments. Environmental cell (S)TEM holders offer powerful functionality including liquid flow, electrochemical cycling and heating in gas environments. However, in these environmental cell holders the SiNx windows needed to separate the sample and liquid or gas environment from the instrument vacuum reduces the signal to noise ratio (SNR), degrades the achievable energy resolution for spectroscopy and limits the spatial resolution for imaging [1-3]. Graphene (S)TEM liquid cells offer improved resolution due to the reduced scattering from the use of ultra-thin graphene as the window material. Yet the presence of liquid will still add a background that can degrade the SNR. This is especially important since reducing the electron beam flux is highly desirable as it will minimize the potential for radiolytic changes to occur in the liquid or gas environment. Such changes are best understood for aqueous systems where radiolytic evolution results in many potentially active species and can result in dramatic changes to the pH [4]. Imaging under ultra low dose conditions in the presence of low SNR is therefore highly desirable, as long as it does not prevent the necessary data being extracted from the images.
